newsitem.title: UK: Foreign, defence policies ignored in UK election.
newsitem.headline: Foreign, defence policies ignored in UK election.

text.p: Blink and you've missed it.

Britain may be a major trading nation and a permanent member of the U.N. Security Council, but it seems the two major parties contesting the May 1 election would be happiest if voters ignored foreign and defence affairs altogether.
In the 58-page manifesto issued by the ruling Conservatives, foreign policy first raises its head on page 45. Defence policy takes over on page 47 and ends just seven paragraphs later.
The opposition Labour party is even less interested, devoting less than three pages of text to the two issues at the very back of its manifesto.

While such caution might be understandable for a small landlocked European state, it does not fit comfortably with Britain's cherished tradition of "punching above its weight" -- exerting a disproportionately large influence for its size.
"The entire foreign policy is to avoid having a foreign policy," said Dr Jonathan Eyal, director of studies at the Royal United Services Institute think-tank.

"In general, there is complete agreement between both Labour and the Conservatives that while a great foreign policy failure might lose an election, foreign policy successes do not win elections," he said in a telephone interview.
Little seems to divide the two parties, who talk in general terms about keeping Britain's defence strong, playing a leading role and helping reform the United Nations.
The similarity of approaches testifies to Labour leader Tony Blair's efforts to ditch many of the left-wing policies which provided such easy targets in the past for the Conservatives.

Old-style Labour adopted an avowedly internationalist and moralistic tone -- its 1983 manifesto devoted separate sections to the Near and Middle East, Africa, Latin America, Asia, the Commonwealth and even the international Law of the Sea.
But voters did not like the party's promise to quit the European Union and unilaterally scrap Britain's nuclear weapons, which laid Labour open to charges that it was soft on communism.

The job of Foreign Secretary is one of the most high-profile posts in British politics, but from the manifestos at least, it is hard to figure what the next incumbent will be doing outside deciding the tricky question of Britain's stance towards Europe.
"The whole issue has been emasculated by both parties because you can't run a foreign policy without money and no one wants to talk about spending money in the run-up to an election," said Eyal.

The only issue which merits more than a mention in either document is future relations with the European Union, but both parties are suitably vague about an issue capable of causing deep spilts on both sides of the political divide.
"There seems to be almost a conspiracy of silence on behalf of the two parties, essentially in that both want to tiptoe around the issue. It is too much of a hot potato," said Eyal.
Foreign policy experts lament what they see as both parties' deliberate marginalisation of foreign affairs.

"They should be discussing the role of the United Nations in conflict avoidance, how we can prevent tragedies like Burundi and Zaire from happening," said Malcolm Harper, director of the United Nations Association (UNA) all-party lobby group.

"These matters do have a direct influence on British interests, whether they either affect our trade or whether we have to send in troops to restore order somewhere in the world," he said by telephone.
The UNA wants the new government to raise the amount spent on overseas aid to the U.N. target of 0.7 percent of Gross National Product. The Conservatives now spend 0.26 percent.

Richard Gott, a political observer with the Independent newspaper, despaired at the lack of discussion on major issues such as relations with China, how to solve the protracted Middle East crisis and the best approach to take over NATO expansion.
"During the entire campaign we shall hear nothing of these issues. Yet they will not go away just because no one is looking," he wrote on Tuesday.

"History also tells us that a newly elected prime minister, once in government, soon finds much of his or her time caught up in the minutiae of foreign affairs -- for better or sometimes for worse," he said.
